candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'reveal what is omitted' and the occupational therapist viewpoint pointed to what surgical consent often leaves out: what daily activities will look like during recovery.
candidates.working_title: Ask what a normal day looks like three months after surgery
candidates.core_insight: Before a major operation, an older person can ask the surgical team to describe what everyday life is likely to look like during recovery, for example at three months, which a discussion of operative complications usually leaves out.
candidates.angle: Consent conversations list what can go wrong in and just after theatre; for many older people the deciding question is whether they will be able to wash, dress, walk outside and live where they live now, and how long getting back to that takes.
candidates.position: Older people facing major surgery should be told the likely course of recovery of daily function as well as the operative risks, and they are entitled to ask for it.
claims_needing_evidence: Recovery of everyday activities after major abdominal surgery in older people often takes months rather than weeks (prospective cohort study).
Many seriously ill older people say they would not choose a treatment if the likely outcome was survival with severe functional or cognitive impairment (interview or survey study).
UK law requires doctors to discuss risks this patient would consider significant and reasonable alternatives, including no treatment (Supreme Court judgment; GMC guidance).
Surgeons' descriptions of high-risk operations to older patients often focus on fixing the problem and on operative risks rather than on recovery (qualitative study).

Finlayson E et al. 2012, J Am Geriatr Soc, functional status after colon cancer surgery in nursing home residents (unsure of details)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Before a major operation, ask the surgeon what a normal day is likely to look like three months afterwards.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: the question in large type, with four small line-drawn panels of the everyday activities to ask about (washing, dressing, walking outside, being at home), and a footer line suggesting the follow-up questions 'What is the best case, the worst case, and the most likely?'
candidates.pause: Families recognise the gap between 'the operation went well' and 'she has not been able to go home'.
candidates.gain: One specific question that brings the recovery of daily life into the decision, which is often what decides whether an operation is worth it for the person.
candidates.follow: The account gives questions people can use in real decisions, without scaremongering about surgery.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E116 (tell the surgical team who the person was last week) and E109 (getting home after hip fracture depends on thinking, standing, eating and toileting). This post is about asking for the likely recovery course before any major operation, not about hip fracture or baseline.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the scale' with 'stopwatch' and 'five years' prompted moving from trial results gathered across hundreds of people over years to one person's question: how long before this could help me?
candidates.working_title: Every preventive treatment has a waiting time
candidates.core_insight: Screening tests and preventive medicines take time before they help anyone, while their inconvenience and side effects can start straight away, so how long a person is likely to live and what they want from that time belong in the decision.
candidates.angle: Trials report benefit across many people over several years; from one person's side, the useful question is how long before this is likely to help, and whether that is time they expect to have and want to spend this way. The waits differ widely between treatments.
candidates.position: Time to benefit should be part of every preventive treatment and screening decision in later life, weighed against the person's health, likely life expectancy and goals; age alone should not decide it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a meta-analysis of screening trials, about [N to verify] years passed before 1 death from breast or bowel cancer was prevented per 1000 people screened (meta-analysis of randomised trial survival data).
In statin primary prevention trials in adults aged 50 to 75, about [N to verify] years passed before 1 major cardiovascular event was prevented per 100 people treated (meta-analysis).
In bisphosphonate trials in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, about [N to verify] months passed before 1 non-vertebral fracture was prevented per 100 women treated (meta-analysis).
Harms of screening (for example colonoscopy complications, overdiagnosis) and of medicines can occur soon after starting (review).
evidence_leads: Lee SJ et al. 2013, BMJ 346:e8441, time lag to benefit after screening for breast and colorectal cancer
Yourman LC et al. 2021, JAMA Intern Med 181:179-85, time to benefit of statins for primary prevention
Deardorff WJ et al. 2022, JAMA Intern Med 182:33-41, time to benefit of bisphosphonates
Lee SJ, Leipzig RM, Walter LC 2013, JAMA 310:2609-10, incorporating lag time to benefit into prevention decisions for older adults
Holmes HM et al. 2006, Arch Intern Med 166:605-09, reconsidering medication appropriateness late in life
Time to benefit of intensive blood pressure lowering in older adults, Lee SJ group, JAMA Intern Med about 2024 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Every screening test and preventive medicine has a waiting time before it helps anyone.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram: a horizontal axis in years; a band starting at year 0 labelled 'tests, appointments and possible side effects start now'; below it, one labelled marker per treatment showing when trials showed benefit, each with its own denominator written beside it (per 100 or per 1000 people), so treatments are not placed on a false common scale. Credit line to the meta-analyses.
candidates.pause: Most people have never been told that a preventive treatment has a waiting time, and the range from about a year to about a decade is surprising.
candidates.gain: A concept they can use in any prevention decision: ask how long before benefit, and set that against their health and priorities.
candidates.follow: It explains decisions that are usually presented as fixed rules.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none (E090 and E100 argue for bone treatment; this post is about time to benefit as a general idea across treatments)

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' with the viewpoint 'a researcher designing a trial' led to reading a blood pressure trial from its designers' side: who was left out to make the result clean.
candidates.working_title: Read the exclusion list before applying the target
candidates.core_insight: The main trial behind lower blood pressure targets excluded people living in care homes and people with dementia, so applying its target to them is an extrapolation that needs judgement.
candidates.angle: Trial results are quoted without their exclusion lists; reading the list tells you whether the person in front of you resembles the people who were studied. In the same trial, fit older people aged 75 and over did benefit, so the lesson cuts both ways.
candidates.position: For older people outside the trial populations, blood pressure treatment should be guided by standing blood pressure, falls, symptoms and the person's goals rather than a target from trials that excluded them; this is no reason to withhold treatment from fit older people, in whom the trials showed benefit.
claims_needing_evidence: SPRINT excluded people with diabetes, prior stroke, dementia, nursing home residence, and standing systolic blood pressure below 110 mmHg (trial publication and protocol).
In SPRINT participants aged 75 and over, intensive treatment reduced major cardiovascular events and death, including in participants classed as frail by a frailty index (subgroup publication).
HYVET enrolled people aged 80 and over and excluded people needing nursing care and people with dementia (trial publication).
NICE NG136 advises clinical judgement for people with frailty or multimorbidity when setting blood pressure targets (guideline).
evidence_leads: SPRINT Research Group 2015, NEJM 373:2103-16
Williamson JD et al. 2016, JAMA 315:2673-82, SPRINT participants aged 75 and over
Beckett NS et al. 2008, NEJM 358:1887-98, HYVET
NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults (2019, updated 2023)
Benetos A et al. 2015, JAMA Intern Med, PARTAGE, observational cohort of nursing home residents (unsure of details; observational only)
candidates.opening_line_draft: The trial behind lower blood pressure targets did not enrol people living in care homes or people with a diagnosis of dementia.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated document: a drawn trial eligibility page with the verified exclusion criteria listed and marked with burnt orange underlines and text labels (care home, dementia, standing systolic below 110, diabetes, previous stroke); beside it two labelled columns, 'Who was studied' and 'Who you may be treating'. Credit line SPRINT NEJM 2015.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who apply targets daily may never have read the exclusion list; seeing care homes and dementia on it is a surprise.
candidates.gain: A habit (read who was excluded) and a practical approach for older people outside the trial population.
candidates.follow: Careful reading of evidence applied to everyday prescribing.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'trace a handover between people or services' with the GP viewpoint followed a hospital decision to stop a medicine as it travels to general practice, where the reason often does not arrive; 'aviation checklists' suggested a three-field template.
candidates.working_title: When you stop a treatment, write down why
candidates.core_insight: A decision to stop or withhold a treatment survives the handover to the next team only if the letter records the reason, what would justify restarting, and who will review it.
candidates.angle: Discharge letters often record that a medicine was stopped but not why, which leaves the GP or the next admitting team to guess, and a treatment stopped for a good reason can be restarted by default.
candidates.position: Every stopped or withheld treatment in a discharge letter should carry a one-line reason, a restart condition and a named reviewer.
claims_needing_evidence: Hospital discharge summaries frequently omit essential information, including reasons for medication changes (systematic review or audit).
Medicines stopped in hospital are sometimes restarted after discharge without a new decision (observational study).
Incomplete communication of medication changes at discharge is linked with medication errors after discharge (systematic review).
evidence_leads: Kripalani S et al. 2007, JAMA 297:831-41, deficits in communication and information transfer between hospital-based and primary care physicians
Professional Record Standards Body, eDischarge summary standard, medication change and reason fields (unsure)
Royal Pharmaceutical Society 2012, Keeping patients safe when they transfer between care providers (unsure)
Studies of persistence of hospital deprescribing after discharge (unsure; needs search)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A discharge letter that says 'amlodipine stopped' records a decision without its reason.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card labelled 'Illustrative example': two versions of the same discharge letter line. Left: 'Amlodipine stopped.' Right: the same line with three added fields: reason, restart only if, reviewed by. Footer with author name and series.
candidates.pause: GPs and hospital doctors have all seen a stopped medicine reappear, and they recognise the one-line letter.
candidates.gain: A three-field template that helps treatment decisions survive handover.
candidates.follow: Specific, practical improvements to everyday clinical paperwork.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E142 (medication review after delirium as a named task) and E079 (what a falls clinic referral should contain). This post is about recording reasons and restart conditions for any stopped or withheld treatment.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses' with the viewpoint 'a researcher designing a trial' and 'a decade' pointed to prevention trials that chose disability-free survival as their main outcome.
candidates.working_title: A trial that counted years lived without disability
candidates.core_insight: ASPREE, a large trial of daily aspirin in healthy older people, made its main outcome whether people stayed alive without dementia or lasting physical disability; aspirin did not improve it and increased serious bleeding.
candidates.angle: Most prevention trials count heart attacks and strokes; ASPREE counted the outcome older people usually say they want, and that choice changed what the result means for them. It applies to people without heart disease or stroke, not to people taking aspirin after one.
candidates.position: Trials of preventive treatment in older people should report disability-free survival alongside disease events; ASPREE shows why.
claims_needing_evidence: ASPREE randomised [N to verify] community-dwelling people aged 70 and over (65 and over for US Black and Hispanic participants) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability to aspirin 100 mg or placebo (NEJM 2018).
Aspirin did not prolong disability-free survival over a median follow-up of about [N to verify] years (NEJM 2018).
Major haemorrhage was more common with aspirin (NEJM 2018).
All-cause mortality was higher with aspirin, mainly from cancer, a finding the authors advised interpreting with caution (NEJM 2018).
People taking aspirin after a heart attack or stroke should not stop it without medical advice (guideline or NHS information).
Other trials in older people, such as STAREE and PREVENTABLE for statins, use disability-free or dementia-free survival as main outcomes (trial registrations or protocols).

candidates.opening_line_draft: A trial of daily aspirin in [N to verify] healthy people aged 70 and over had one main outcome: staying alive without dementia or lasting disability.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: one horizontal bar labelled 'disability-free survival', with three labelled end points that stop it (death, dementia, persistent physical disability); a second panel states both groups' results in words and verified figures, including the bleeding result. candidates.gain: The public learn what disability-free survival means and why aspirin for prevention in healthy older people is not recommended; practitioners get an outcome to look for in trials.
candidates.follow: The account explains which outcomes a trial counted, not only its headline.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome patients value' with 'wall calendar' and 'the moment of discharge' suggested counting the days a person spends at home in the month after discharge or surgery.
candidates.working_title: Count the days at home
candidates.core_insight: Days alive and at home after an operation or admission capture readmissions, rehabilitation stays and new care home moves that length of stay and 30-day mortality miss.
candidates.angle: A service can shorten length of stay and keep mortality low while patients spend much of the following month back in hospital or in a rehabilitation bed; a 30-day calendar makes this visible, and validated measures already exist.
candidates.position: Hospitals and surgical services caring for older people should report days alive and at home alongside mortality and length of stay.
claims_needing_evidence: Days alive and at home within 30 days after surgery (DAH30) has been validated and is associated with patient-reported disability and complications (prospective cohort study).
Days alive and out of hospital has been validated in large population administrative data for perioperative outcomes (validation study).
Home time can be measured from routine claims data and relates to other outcomes in older adults (validation study).
Length of stay does not include days in other hospitals, rehabilitation units or readmissions (definition used in routine statistics).

candidates.visual_idea: Calendar comparison labelled 'Illustrative example': two 30-day grids for two people with the same 5-day length of stay; one then has 25 days at home, the other a readmission and a rehabilitation stay. candidates.pause: The calendar makes a familiar performance measure look incomplete at a glance.
candidates.gain: A named, validated outcome they can propose for audit or service evaluation.
candidates.follow: It questions how services measure success and offers measures that are ready to use.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses' with 'hidden cost' and 'packing' pointed to the time a treatment takes: days spent travelling to, waiting for and attending care.
candidates.working_title: Ask how many days a month a treatment will take
candidates.core_insight: The time a treatment takes, counted as days with appointments, tests, infusions, travel and waiting, is a real cost to older people and their families, and it can be asked about before agreeing.
candidates.angle: Cancer researchers now count 'contact days', days with any contact with health services, because survival figures do not show how much of the remaining time treatment uses. The same question applies to any treatment with frequent visits.
candidates.position: Older people are entitled to know how many days a treatment is likely to take from their month, and clinicians should offer that information when discussing options.
claims_needing_evidence: 'Time toxicity' and 'contact days' have been proposed as outcomes of cancer treatment (peer-reviewed commentary).
Secondary analyses of cancer trials have measured contact days and found they can take up a substantial share of days alive (secondary trial analysis).
In-centre haemodialysis usually involves three sessions a week of about four hours, plus travel (NHS or kidney charity information).

candidates.visual_idea: Question card: a month calendar with some days marked by a small clinic symbol and a text label, and three questions beside it: How many days a month? How much travel and waiting? Who will need to come with me?
candidates.pause: Older people and carers know the cost of hospital days and transport, but rarely hear it treated as part of the decision.

candidates.stimulus_use: The same draw's speech and language therapist viewpoint and 'the last week of life' suggested an outcome that aspiration risk misses: the pleasure and dignity of eating and drinking, and the shared decision to continue with acknowledged risk.
candidates.working_title: Eating and drinking with acknowledged risks
candidates.core_insight: When swallowing becomes unsafe and treatment will not make it safe, continuing to eat and drink with the risks understood and planned for is a recognised choice made with the person, and nil by mouth or heavily modified diets carry harms of their own.
candidates.angle: The routine measure is aspiration risk; the person may put more value on taste, pleasure, company at mealtimes and comfort. National guidance now describes how teams and families can plan this together.
candidates.position: For people whose swallowing difficulty will not improve with treatment, especially near the end of life, eating and drinking with acknowledged risks should be offered as a supported option through shared decision-making, and should not be regarded as neglect or as giving up.
claims_needing_evidence: The Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists published multidisciplinary guidance on eating and drinking with acknowledged risks in 2021 (professional guidance).
Thickened fluids reduce aspiration seen on swallowing studies, but trials have not shown a clear reduction in pneumonia (randomised trial or systematic review).
Thickened fluids are associated with lower fluid intake or poorer acceptance in some studies (observational studies or review).
Royal College of Physicians guidance supports careful hand feeding for people with eating and drinking difficulties near the end of life (professional guidance).
evidence_leads: RCSLT 2021, Eating and drinking with acknowledged risks: multidisciplinary team guidance for the shared decision-making process (adults)
Royal College of Physicians 2021, Supporting people who have eating and drinking difficulties
Robbins J et al. 2008, Ann Intern Med 148:509-18, two interventions for liquid aspiration and pneumonia incidence
Cichero JAY 2013, Nutrition Journal, thickened fluids and hydration (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: When swallowing becomes unsafe, continuing to eat and drink with the risks understood and planned for is a recognised option.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison diagram: three columns (no food or drink by mouth with other feeding; modified diet and thickened fluids; eating and drinking with acknowledged risks) and the same rows for each (what it aims to prevent, what it costs the person, what support it needs), with text only from verified guidance.
candidates.pause: Families who have seen a relative put on thickened fluids or nil by mouth may not know another planned option exists.
candidates.gain: Understanding of a legitimate option and the words to ask for a shared decision.
candidates.follow: It treats pleasure and comfort as outcomes worth counting.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E187 (aspiration and delirium: do not thicken the diet and miss the pneumonia). This post is about the shared decision to continue eating with acknowledged risk. Possible overlap with C13 (swallowing), to be resolved at allocation.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find the first question worth asking' with 'forecasting' and 'the first hour' led to how a serious treatment conversation should open: with the person's understanding and hopes, before options or forecasts.
candidates.working_title: Open with what the person understands
candidates.core_insight: Structured serious illness conversations start by asking what the person understands about their health and how much they want to know, then share information, then discuss goals, worries and trade-offs.
candidates.angle: Clinicians often open treatment discussions with the options; asking first what the person already understands shows where to begin, brings misunderstandings out early, and makes the rest of the discussion shorter and more relevant.
candidates.position: In serious treatment decisions with older people, the first question should be about the person's understanding and how much information they want, before any treatment is described.
claims_needing_evidence: The Serious Illness Conversation Guide opens with questions about the patient's understanding of their illness and their information preferences (published guide).
In a cluster randomised trial in oncology, the Serious Illness Care Program led to more, earlier and better-quality documented conversations (trial secondary analysis).
The same trial did not show a significant difference in its primary outcome, goal-concordant care, but reduced moderate to severe anxiety and depression symptoms (trial publication).

Paladino J et al. 2019, JAMA Oncol 5:801-09, conversation quality in the same trial

candidates.pause: Practitioners recognise the stalled conversation that began with a list of treatment options.
candidates.gain: An opening sequence they can use on the next ward round or clinic.
candidates.follow: Teaching points that are specific, sourced and usable.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'look at the smallest practical detail' with 'aviation checklists' drew attention to one measurement step in blood pressure decisions: the standing reading.
candidates.working_title: Base the target on the standing reading
candidates.core_insight: NICE advises measuring standing as well as seated blood pressure in people with hypertension aged 80 and over, and treating to a target based on standing blood pressure when there is a significant postural drop.
candidates.angle: A seated clinic reading can show blood pressure above target in a person whose pressure falls when they stand; treating to the seated number then adds to dizziness and falls.
candidates.position: No decision to start or increase blood pressure treatment in a person aged 80 or over should be made without a standing reading.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG136 recommends measuring blood pressure seated or supine and standing in people with hypertension who have type 2 diabetes, symptoms of postural hypotension, or are aged 80 and over (guideline).
NICE NG136 recommends that people with a significant postural drop or symptoms of postural hypotension are treated to a target based on standing blood pressure (guideline).
NICE NG136 clinic blood pressure target for people aged 80 and over is below 150/90 mmHg (guideline).
Orthostatic hypotension is common in older people (meta-analysis of prevalence).
evidence_leads: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management (2019, updated 2023)
Saedon NI et al. 2020, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci, prevalence of orthostatic hypotension in older adults, meta-analysis (unsure)
Juraschek SP et al. 2020, Hypertension, intensive blood pressure treatment and orthostatic hypotension, meta-analysis (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: For anyone aged 80 or over with high blood pressure, NICE advises a standing reading as well as a sitting one.
candidates.visual_idea: Flow diagram: seated reading and standing reading (values labelled 'Illustrative example'), then a decision point 'significant drop or symptoms on standing?', leading to 'treat to the standing reading'; includes the NICE timing for the standing measurement once verified.
candidates.pause: Many clinicians treat the seated number by habit; the NICE wording is specific and easy to quote.
candidates.gain: A concrete step, with its guideline source, that prevents overtreatment.
candidates.follow: Small, sourced changes to everyday practice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E069 (standing blood pressure after falls, family audience). This post is about using the standing reading to set the treatment target in all people aged 80 and over with hypertension, whether or not they have fallen.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'look at what happens at night or at the weekend' with the viewpoint 'a spouse of 50 years' led to the out-of-hours decision made by a clinician who has never met the person, with a husband or wife asked on the spot what the person would want.
candidates.working_title: Will the doctor at 3am know what you would want?
candidates.core_insight: Wishes about emergency treatment help at night or at the weekend only if they are recorded where out-of-hours doctors, ambulance crews and hospitals can see them, such as a Key Information Summary in Scotland or a ReSPECT form.
candidates.angle: Crisis decisions are often made by clinicians who do not know the person, with a spouse asked what they would want; a plan made earlier with the GP is how the person's own view reaches that moment, whether they want more treatment or less.
candidates.position: Older people who have views about emergency treatment, in either direction, should ask for them to be recorded in the shared record their area uses, and should review it when their health changes.
claims_needing_evidence: In Scotland, the Key Information Summary is created in GP practices and can be seen by out-of-hours services, NHS 24, the Scottish Ambulance Service and hospitals (NHS Scotland or Healthcare Improvement Scotland information).
ReSPECT is a process and form, used in many parts of the UK, that records personalised recommendations for emergency care and treatment (Resuscitation Council UK).
Anticipatory care plans can record wishes to receive treatment as well as to avoid it (NHS Inform or Healthcare Improvement Scotland guidance).
evidence_leads: NHS Inform and Healthcare Improvement Scotland pages on anticipatory care planning and the Key Information Summary
Resuscitation Council UK, ReSPECT

candidates.opening_line_draft: If you became seriously unwell at 3am, the doctor or paramedic deciding what to do might never have met you.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'take a common shortcut and qualify it' with the GP viewpoint pointed to a shortcut in general practice: offering a statin whenever the 10-year QRISK score is above 10%. 'Permission' fed the angle that the score should open a discussion rather than close it.
candidates.working_title: QRISK above 10% at 78
candidates.core_insight: At older ages, age alone puts most people above the 10% QRISK threshold, so the threshold no longer separates who is likely to benefit; the statin decision then rests on time to benefit, other illnesses, frailty and the person's preferences.
candidates.angle: The 10% rule sorts people reasonably well in middle age and loses that ability in later life, where the score mainly reflects age. Evidence for statins in primary prevention over 75 is also thinner.
candidates.position: For people over about 75, a QRISK result above 10% should start a discussion about statins, not settle it.
claims_needing_evidence: QRISK3 was derived and validated for people aged 25 to 84 (BMJ 2017).
At ages above about 75, most people have a QRISK3 10-year risk above 10% even with favourable blood pressure and cholesterol and no smoking (calculator worked examples or a published analysis).
NICE NG238 recommends QRISK3 for people up to 84 and advises considering atorvastatin 20 mg for people 85 and over, taking account of comorbidity, frailty and life expectancy (guideline).
Direct trial evidence for statins in primary prevention in people over 75 is more limited than for people with vascular disease (individual participant meta-analysis).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'reveal what is omitted' with the quality 'reversibility' pointed to a feature of treatment choices that is rarely said out loud: whether the choice can be tried and undone.
candidates.working_title: Can this choice be undone?
candidates.core_insight: Some treatment choices can be tried and stopped if they do not help, and others are hard or impossible to reverse; knowing which kind a decision is tells you how much time and information it needs.
candidates.angle: Discussions of options rarely state whether a choice is reversible, yet a reversible choice can often be tried with a review date, while an irreversible one deserves more questions and more time before it is made.
candidates.position: Older people and families should ask whether a treatment choice can be reversed; when it can, trying it with a review date is often a reasonable way to decide.
claims_needing_evidence: GMC guidance states there is no legal or necessary morally relevant difference between withholding and withdrawing a treatment, although stopping may feel harder (GMC guidance).
Time-limited trials of treatment are an established approach in serious illness (peer-reviewed literature).
The generic examples used (a medicine can usually be stopped and restarted; a major operation is not reversible) are accurate (clinical reasoning; no statistic).
evidence_leads: GMC 2010, Treatment and care towards the end of life: good practice in decision making (withholding and withdrawing)
Quill TE, Holloway R 2011, JAMA 306:1483-84, time-limited trials near the end of life
NICE NG197 Shared decision making (2021)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Some treatment choices can be tried and undone. Others are hard or impossible to reverse. Before choosing, it helps to know which kind this is.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: two columns labelled 'Can be tried and stopped' and 'Hard or impossible to undo', each with two or three accurate generic examples, and a question along the bottom: 'If we try this and it is not helping, what happens then?'
candidates.pause: The distinction is simple, new to many people, and usable at once.
candidates.gain: A way to judge how much time a decision needs, and a question to ask.
candidates.follow: Clear thinking tools for treatment decisions.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' with the viewpoint 'a ward clerk' and 'the first month' led to the view from the desk that books follow-up: the number of appointments a person with several conditions leaves hospital with.
candidates.working_title: Count the appointments before booking them
candidates.core_insight: For older people with several conditions, each follow-up appointment costs travel, waiting, energy and often a relative's time, so each should be justified by a decision it could change, and several can sometimes be combined.
candidates.angle: Services record appointments as activity; the person experiences them as work. NICE multimorbidity guidance asks clinicians to assess and reduce treatment burden, including appointments, and to agree who coordinates care.
candidates.position: Before discharge or at the end of a clinic, someone should count the person's planned appointments and ask which will change a decision; the rest should be combined, moved to one clinician, or cancelled with the person's agreement.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG56 recommends assessing treatment burden in people with multimorbidity, including healthcare appointments, and agreeing who is responsible for coordinating care (guideline).
People with multimorbidity report attending multiple appointments as part of their treatment burden (qualitative and questionnaire studies).
Higher treatment burden is associated with poorer quality of life and lower adherence (systematic review or cohort study).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare what is recorded with what is experienced' with 'rhythm' pointed to the gap between one blood pressure recorded in clinic and blood pressure through an ordinary day.
candidates.working_title: The surgery reading and the home reading
candidates.core_insight: Blood pressure is often higher in clinic than at home, so NICE recommends home or 24-hour readings to confirm high blood pressure, and older people can ask whether their treatment is based on them.
candidates.angle: A clinic reading records one moment; home readings show what blood pressure does in daily life. For older people, especially those who feel dizzy, treatment decisions are safer when home readings are part of them.
candidates.position: Before starting or increasing blood pressure tablets, older people should ask whether the decision is based on home or 24-hour readings, and can bring their own home readings to appointments.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG136 recommends ambulatory (24-hour) monitoring, or home monitoring if ambulatory monitoring is unsuitable, to confirm hypertension when clinic blood pressure is between 140/90 and 180/120 mmHg (guideline).
Clinic readings are often higher than home readings (white-coat effect), and this is common in older people (cohort study or review).
NICE targets for people aged 80 and over are below 150/90 mmHg in clinic and below 145/85 mmHg at home or on ambulatory monitoring (guideline).
Some people have higher readings at home than in clinic (masked hypertension) (review).

candidates.stimulus_use: The same draw's physiotherapist viewpoint and 'the first hour' suggested the moment an older person says no to a treatment, and the single word the notes record.
candidates.working_title: Write down why the person said no
candidates.core_insight: When an older person declines a treatment, recording their reasons in their own words, checking what they understood, noting whether pain, fear, hearing or timing played a part, and offering to revisit respects the decision and catches reasons that can be addressed.
candidates.angle: 'Declined' records a decision without its reason; the reason is what the next clinician needs, either to respect the choice without re-arguing it or to address a problem behind it.
candidates.position: A person with capacity has the right to decline treatment; the notes should record their reasons and what was offered, so the decision is respected and is not mistaken for a misunderstanding or a bad moment.
claims_needing_evidence: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, adults are presumed to have capacity, and an unwise decision alone does not show a lack of capacity (legislation and codes of practice).
GMC guidance says doctors must respect a patient's decision to decline treatment and should explore the patient's concerns and reasons (GMC guidance).
Correctable factors such as hearing impairment, pain and the timing of a conversation can affect a person's ability to take part in decisions (guidance or studies).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 1 principles
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, general principles
GMC 2020, Decision making and consent
NICE NG197 Shared decision making (2021)

candidates.pause: Practitioners write or read 'declined' daily and rarely think about what it leaves out.
candidates.gain: A documentation habit that protects both the person's right to decide and their access to care.
candidates.follow: Practical teaching that respects older people's decisions.

candidates.working_title: When screening invitations stop, symptoms still need checking
candidates.core_insight: Routine screening invitations end at set ages, but a new symptom such as a lump, bleeding or a change in bowel habit needs a GP appointment at any age, and some screening can still be requested after the invitations stop.
candidates.angle: Older people can read the end of screening letters as the end of being checked. Screening is for people without symptoms, and its age limits reflect the balance of benefit and harm across a population; they say nothing about symptoms or about a person's worth.
candidates.position: The end of screening invitations should come with clear information about symptoms to report and about self-referral where it exists.
claims_needing_evidence: NHS breast screening in England invites women from 50 up to their 71st birthday, and women over 71 can ask for screening every three years (NHS website).
NHS bowel screening in England invites people aged 50 to 74, and people aged 75 and over can request a kit (NHS website).
Scottish screening programmes' age ranges and self-referral arrangements (NHS Inform).
More than [N to verify] of new cancer cases in the UK are diagnosed in people aged 75 and over (Cancer Research UK statistics).
Screening tests are for people without symptoms; people with symptoms need diagnostic assessment (UK National Screening Committee or NHS information).

NHS Inform (Scotland) screening pages
UK National Screening Committee
Cancer Research UK, cancer incidence by age
candidates.opening_line_draft: Screening letters stop at a set age. A new lump, bleeding or a change in bowel habit still needs a GP appointment, whatever your age.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram: an age axis from 50 to 90 with verified invitation ranges for each programme shown as labelled bars ending at their stop ages; beneath them a continuous line along the whole axis labelled 'New symptoms: see your GP at any age', plus a short note on self-referral.

candidates.follow: Clear explanations of how services work for older people.

candidates.working_title: How to talk about stopping screening
candidates.core_insight: Older adults in US studies were often open to stopping cancer screening but disliked being told they might not live long enough to benefit, preferring explanations based on their other health priorities and the balance of benefit and harm.
candidates.angle: The clinical reason for stopping may be limited life expectancy, but the words used can make the same advice feel like being written off; research has tested which phrasings older people find acceptable.
candidates.position: When advising an older person to stop screening, clinicians should explain it in terms of benefit, harm and the person's other health priorities, and avoid saying they may not live long enough to benefit.
claims_needing_evidence: In interviews with older adults, many were willing to stop screening and saw their clinician's recommendation as important (qualitative study).

In a national US survey of older adults, 'you may not live long enough to benefit from this test' was among the least preferred explanations, and explanations based on health priorities or lack of benefit were preferred (survey study).
Some older people with limited life expectancy continue to be screened (observational study).
evidence_leads: Schoenborn NL et al. 2017, JAMA Intern Med 177:1121-28, older adults' views and communication preferences about cancer screening cessation
Schoenborn NL et al. 2018, JAMA Oncol, preferred clinician communication about stopping cancer screening, national survey (unsure of details)
Royce TJ et al. 2014, JAMA Intern Med, cancer screening rates by life expectancy (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Older adults surveyed in the US were often open to stopping cancer screening. What many disliked was being told they might not live long enough to benefit.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: two example phrasings in plain boxes (not attributed to anyone), one marked 'least preferred in the survey' and one 'preferred', with the source line and a label stating these are research findings about wording.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who have used the life-expectancy phrase will recognise it.
candidates.gain: Tested wording for a difficult conversation.
candidates.follow: Evidence-based teaching on communication as well as on drugs and tests.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: At 80, how many years are left?
candidates.core_insight: Average life expectancy at 80 in the UK is close to a decade for women and a little less for men, and the range around the average is wide, so age alone is a poor basis for deciding someone is too old for a treatment.
candidates.angle: People, including clinicians, often underestimate how long healthy older people live. The same age can mean five years or fifteen, depending on health and function.
candidates.position: Treatment decisions in later life should rest on the person's health, function and goals rather than on age alone; ruling out a treatment because of age is not supported by what we know about life expectancy.
claims_needing_evidence: ONS national life tables give period life expectancy at age 80 in the UK of about [N to verify] years for women and [N to verify] years for men (ONS).

Life expectancy at a given older age varies widely: in US life table data, the healthiest quarter of 80-year-olds live several years longer than the median and the least healthy quarter several years shorter (Walter and Covinsky 2001).
Prognostic indices that use health and function predict mortality in older adults better than age alone (systematic review).

Walter LC, Covinsky KE 2001, JAMA 285:2750-56, cancer screening in elderly patients: a framework for individualized decision making (life expectancy quartiles)
Yourman LC et al. 2012, JAMA 307:182-92, prognostic indices for older adults
ePrognosis (UCSF)
candidates.opening_line_draft: In the UK, a woman who reaches 80 can expect, on average, about [N to verify] more years.
candidates.visual_idea: Bar chart from verified data: three horizontal bars for people aged 80 (healthiest quarter, middle, least healthy quarter) showing years remaining, marked as US data from the cited paper, with the UK average from ONS marked separately and labelled.
candidates.pause: The number is larger than many people expect.
candidates.gain: A correction to 'too old for that', and a reason to ask about health rather than age.
candidates.follow: It counters ageism with data rather than slogans.

candidates.working_title: Higher risk, bigger absolute benefit
candidates.core_insight: Because heart attacks and strokes are more common in older people, a treatment with a similar relative effect can prevent more events per 100 people treated at 80 than at 50, provided the person lives long enough to benefit and harms do not rise more.
candidates.angle: Talk of 'less benefit in older people' often mixes up relative and absolute effects. In pooled trials of blood pressure lowering and statins, relative effects were broadly similar across ages, while baseline risk was much higher in older people.
candidates.position: Older age can increase the absolute benefit of some preventive treatments; decisions to withhold them should rest on time to benefit, competing illness, harms and the person's preference, not on age.
claims_needing_evidence: In an individual participant meta-analysis of blood pressure lowering trials, relative reductions in major cardiovascular events were seen across age groups, including people aged 85 and over, with absolute risk reductions similar or larger in older groups (Lancet 2021).

In the CTT meta-analysis, statins produced similar proportional reductions in major vascular events across age groups in people with vascular disease, with less direct evidence for primary prevention over 75 (Lancet 2019).
HYVET showed reductions in stroke, heart failure and death with treatment in people aged 80 and over (NEJM 2008).
evidence_leads: Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists' Collaboration 2021, Lancet 398:1053-64, age-stratified effects of blood pressure lowering
Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration 2019, Lancet 393:407-15
Beckett NS et al. 2008, NEJM 358:1887-98, HYVET
candidates.opening_line_draft: The same relative reduction in stroke risk prevents more strokes among 85-year-olds than among 55-year-olds, because strokes are more common at 85.
candidates.visual_idea: Icon array comparison: two groups of 100 people (aged 55 and aged 85), showing more events without treatment in the older group and the same proportional reduction, so more people spared in absolute terms; labelled 'Illustrative example' unless verified trial figures are used, with a note that this holds only if the person lives long enough and harms do not outweigh it.
candidates.pause: Many assume prevention is less worthwhile in older age; the arithmetic shows why that can be wrong.
candidates.gain: A clear distinction between relative and absolute benefit, applied to older people.
candidates.follow: It teaches how to read effect sizes in the population this account cares about.

candidates.working_title: Material risk for an older patient
candidates.core_insight: Under the Montgomery judgment, a material risk is one a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this particular patient, would consider significant, and for many older people that includes losing independence, a long recovery, or not returning home.
candidates.angle: Consent discussions often list anatomical complications; the legal test points clinicians to what this person would weigh, and requires reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, to be discussed.
candidates.position: For older people, a consent discussion that leaves out risks to independence and the option of not having the treatment falls short of what Montgomery and GMC guidance require.
claims_needing_evidence: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 defined a material risk as one a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to, or that the doctor is or should reasonably be aware this patient would (judgment).
The judgment requires doctors to take reasonable care to inform patients of reasonable alternative or variant treatments (judgment).
GMC guidance says doctors should discuss the option of taking no action (GMC 2020).
Many older people give high priority to outcomes such as independence and cognitive function when weighing treatments (survey or interview studies).
evidence_leads: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11
GMC 2020, Decision making and consent
Fried TR et al. 2002, NEJM 346:1061-66

candidates.opening_line_draft: Since Montgomery, a material risk is one that this patient would consider significant, and for many older people that includes the risk of not going home.
candidates.visual_idea: Statement card: the legal test in plain words, with a short quoted phrase from the judgment and its citation; beneath it, a short list of outcome risks older people often weigh (not going home, a long recovery, needing daily help), labelled as examples to discuss.
candidates.pause: Practitioners know the case name but may not have linked it to older people's priorities.
candidates.gain: A legal and ethical basis for discussing function and the option of no treatment.
candidates.follow: Teaching that links law, ethics and everyday practice.

candidates.working_title: Dialysis or conservative kidney care
candidates.core_insight: For older people with kidney failure, conservative kidney management (care without dialysis that treats symptoms and protects remaining kidney function) is a recognised option alongside dialysis, and for some people with frailty or other serious illness dialysis adds little time while taking up a lot of it.

candidates.position: Older people with advanced kidney disease should be offered a full discussion of both dialysis and conservative kidney management, based on their health, their priorities and the time each option takes.

candidates.working_title: Best case, worst case, most likely
candidates.core_insight: The Best Case/Worst Case tool helps surgeons describe high-risk operations to older people as scenarios of what life will look like in the best, worst and most likely outcomes, with and without surgery, so the person can choose according to what they value.
candidates.angle: Surgeons often frame high-risk surgery as fixing a problem; describing whole outcomes, including recovery and the path without surgery, lets older people weigh what they care about.
candidates.position: For high-risk surgery in older people, clinicians should describe likely outcomes as scenarios of daily life with and without surgery; tools such as Best Case/Worst Case make that practical.

Best Case/Worst Case presents outcomes with and without surgery as narrative scenarios on a simple drawn graphic (JAMA Surg 2017).
Training surgeons in Best Case/Worst Case improved the quality of decision conversations in a pre-post evaluation (JAMA Surg 2017).

candidates.working_title: Setting up a time-limited trial
candidates.core_insight: A time-limited trial is an agreement to give a treatment for a set time with named signs of improvement, a review date and a plan for either result, and it helps avoid both stopping too early and continuing without benefit.
candidates.angle: Many 'let's see how it goes' plans lack the four details that make a trial a trial; writing them down protects the person from both premature withdrawal and open-ended treatment.
candidates.position: When the benefit of a treatment for an older person is uncertain, clinicians should offer a time-limited trial with written signs of improvement, a duration and a review, agreed with the person or family.
claims_needing_evidence: A time-limited trial has been described as an agreement between clinicians and a patient or family to use a treatment for a defined period to see whether the patient improves according to agreed outcomes (JAMA 2011).

In a quality improvement study in intensive care, training in time-limited trials was associated with shorter ICU stays and fewer invasive procedures without a change in hospital mortality (JAMA Intern Med 2021).
A review describes the use and limits of time-limited trials in intensive care (Intensive Care Med 2018).
evidence_leads: Quill TE, Holloway R 2011, JAMA 306:1483-84
Chang DW et al. 2021, JAMA Intern Med 181:786-94
Vink EE et al. 2018, Intensive Care Med 44:1369-77
candidates.opening_line_draft: A time-limited trial needs four things written down: the treatment, how long it will run, what would count as improvement, and what happens if improvement does not come.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card with four labelled boxes (treatment, duration, signs of improvement, plan at review) and one filled-in example labelled 'Illustrative example'.
candidates.pause: Practitioners recognise vague 'see how it goes' plans.
candidates.gain: A four-item structure they can write in the notes today.
candidates.follow: Usable structures for difficult decisions.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Related to C07-13 (public post on reversible choices); this one is the practitioner method.

candidates.working_title: A limit on one treatment is not a limit on care
candidates.core_insight: A decision not to offer one treatment, such as intensive care or CPR, applies only to that treatment; pain relief, other treatments, help with eating, rehabilitation and company should still be offered on their merits, and a good plan says what will be done.
candidates.angle: Treatment limits are sometimes read as a signal to do less of everything; plans that list what will be done alongside what will not help prevent that.
candidates.position: Every treatment limit should be written together with a list of the care that continues, so that a decision about one treatment is never read as a judgement about the person's worth.
claims_needing_evidence: UK joint guidance states that a DNACPR decision applies only to CPR and does not mean other treatment should be withheld (BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN guidance).
CQC found in 2021 that some DNACPR decisions during the pandemic were made or applied inappropriately (CQC report).
In a US study, physicians were less likely to order other treatments for patients with do-not-resuscitate orders (J Am Geriatr Soc 2002).
The ReSPECT form records recommended care and treatment as well as treatments not recommended (Resuscitation Council UK).
evidence_leads: BMA, Resuscitation Council UK, RCN 2016, Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (3rd edition, with later revisions)
CQC 2021, Protect, respect, connect: decisions about living and dying well during COVID-19
Beach MC, Morrison RS 2002, J Am Geriatr Soc 50:2057-61, effect of DNR orders on physician decision-making
Fritz Z et al. 2013, Resuscitation, Universal Form of Treatment Options (unsure)
Resuscitation Council UK, ReSPECT
candidates.opening_line_draft: A decision not to offer intensive care applies to intensive care, and to nothing else.
candidates.visual_idea: Two-column statement card: left column 'Not recommended' with one item; right column 'Continues' with a longer list (pain and symptom relief, antibiotics or fluids if they help, help with eating and drinking, getting up and moving, visits and company, regular review), so the proportions show at a glance.
candidates.pause: Families worried that a form means 'giving up' will recognise the fear; practitioners see a simple correction.
candidates.gain: Reassurance grounded in guidance, and a request to make: ask what will be done.
candidates.follow: It expresses equal dignity through specific care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E124 (frail should not become shorthand for do not bother). This post is about treatment limits and the care that continues. Possible overlap with C19 (CPR decisions), to be resolved at allocation.

candidates.working_title: Muscle aches and statins: what a trial on each person found
candidates.core_insight: In a UK trial where people who had muscle symptoms on statins alternated statin and placebo without knowing which, symptoms were similar in both periods and most chose to restart; statins cause a small share of muscle symptoms, but most are not caused by the statin.
candidates.angle: The trial design let each person test the statin on themselves; the result shows how often symptoms blamed on a medicine also happen on dummy tablets.
candidates.position: Older people who stopped a statin because of aches, and would otherwise want one, can ask about a structured trial on and off; people who decide against statins for other reasons, such as time to benefit or their priorities, are making a legitimate choice.
claims_needing_evidence: StatinWISE included [N to verify] people in England, with a mean age of about [N to verify], who had stopped or were considering stopping statins because of muscle symptoms (BMJ 2021).
Muscle symptom scores did not differ between statin and placebo periods (BMJ 2021).
About two thirds of those who completed the trial said they intended to restart statins (BMJ 2021).

An individual participant meta-analysis of large blinded statin trials found statins cause a small excess of mostly mild muscle symptoms, mainly in the first year, and that most muscle symptoms reported by people taking statins were not due to the statin (Lancet 2022).
evidence_leads: Herrett E et al. 2021, BMJ 372:n135, StatinWISE n-of-1 trials
Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration 2022, Lancet 400:832-45, statins and muscle symptoms
Wood FA et al. 2020, NEJM 383:2182-84, SAMSON trial (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: People who blamed muscle aches on their statin took statin and dummy tablets in alternating months, without knowing which was which.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram of the trial design: a year-long strip of alternating months labelled statin or placebo (with 'blinded' marked), and the verified result stated in words beneath; any symptom line drawn only from verified summary data, otherwise the design alone is shown.
candidates.pause: Many people have stopped statins because of aches and have never heard of this trial.
candidates.gain: Understanding of symptoms that occur with dummy tablets too, and a practical option to test a statin.
candidates.follow: It explains trial designs as well as results.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Possible overlap with C06 (medicines), to be resolved at allocation.

candidates.working_title: When a good HbA1c signals overtreatment
candidates.core_insight: In older people with diabetes and poor health, a low HbA1c achieved with insulin or a sulfonylurea often signals overtreatment, because the risk of low blood sugar and falls is immediate while the benefit of tight control takes years.
candidates.angle: A routine measure (HbA1c at target) is recorded as success while the person may be having episodes of low blood sugar; US data show many older adults in poor health have tight control on drugs that cause hypoglycaemia.
candidates.position: For older people with frailty or limited life expectancy, clinicians should relax HbA1c targets and reduce insulin or sulfonylureas when HbA1c is low, as guidelines advise.
claims_needing_evidence: In US national survey data, a substantial proportion of older adults with diabetes in poor health had HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol), and many of them were treated with insulin or sulfonylureas (JAMA Intern Med 2015).
Hypoglycaemia in older people is associated with falls, fractures and emergency admissions (observational studies).
Guidelines recommend individualised, less stringent HbA1c targets for older people with frailty or limited life expectancy (ADA Standards of Care; UK guidance on diabetes and frailty; NICE NG28).
The benefits of intensive glucose control on complications take many years to appear (long-term trial follow-up).
evidence_leads: Lipska KJ et al. 2015, JAMA Intern Med 175:356-62, potential overtreatment of diabetes in older adults
Strain WD et al. 2018, Diabet Med 35:838-45, national collaborative statement on type 2 diabetes in older people and frailty (unsure)
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care, Older Adults section (latest edition)
NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults
Holman RR et al. 2008, NEJM 359:1577-89, UKPDS 10-year follow-up
candidates.opening_line_draft: In an older person with frailty, a low HbA1c on insulin or a sulfonylurea can be a sign of overtreatment.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison: two timelines side by side, 'possible harms' (low blood sugar episodes, falls) starting at once and 'benefits of tight control' appearing after years, with verified time frames; a small box listing the drug classes that cause hypoglycaemia.
candidates.pause: Diabetes reviews reward low numbers; the reversal surprises many clinicians.
candidates.gain: A prompt to check the drug class and the HbA1c together, and to reduce treatment where appropriate.
candidates.follow: It questions routine measures with evidence.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Possible overlap with C06 (high-risk medicines), to be resolved at allocation.

candidates.working_title: No upper age limit for emergency stroke treatment
candidates.core_insight: Trials of clot-busting treatment for stroke included many people over 80 and showed benefit in them, and UK stroke guidance sets no upper age limit, so anyone with stroke symptoms should call 999 at once, whatever their age.
candidates.angle: Families, and sometimes staff, may assume emergency stroke treatments are for younger people; the trial evidence says age alone should not exclude anyone.
candidates.position: Age alone should never be the reason an older person is not assessed for emergency stroke treatment; call 999 immediately for stroke symptoms at any age.
claims_needing_evidence: In IST-3, [N to verify] of participants were over 80 (Lancet 2012).
An individual patient data meta-analysis found that alteplase given within 4.5 hours benefited people over 80 to a similar degree as younger people (Lancet 2014).
A pooled analysis of thrombectomy trials found benefit in people aged 80 and over (Lancet 2016).
The National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland (2023) recommends thrombolysis irrespective of age when other criteria are met (guideline wording to check).
evidence_leads: IST-3 collaborative group 2012, Lancet 379:2352-63
Emberson J et al. 2014, Lancet 384:1929-35
Goyal M et al. 2016, Lancet 387:1723-31, HERMES pooled analysis
Intercollegiate Stroke Working Party 2023, National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland
candidates.opening_line_draft: In the largest trial of clot-busting treatment for stroke, more than half of the people treated were over 80.
candidates.visual_idea: Statement card with a verified icon array showing the proportion of IST-3 participants over 80, and beneath it the FAST signs with '999' in large type.
candidates.pause: Families assume older people are not offered emergency stroke treatment; the fact reverses that assumption.
candidates.gain: Confidence to call 999 immediately, and a question to ask about whether emergency treatment was considered.
candidates.follow: It counters ageist assumptions with trial evidence.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Patient Priorities Care: two questions
candidates.core_insight: Patient Priorities Care helps older people with several conditions name specific goals and the care they are willing and able to do, and clinicians then align treatment with them; in a non-randomised trial it was associated with lower perceived treatment burden and fewer unwanted treatments.
candidates.angle: Instead of treating each disease to its own target, the approach starts from what the person wants to be able to do and which care tasks they will accept, and uses that to decide what to start, continue or stop.
candidates.position: For older people with several conditions, specific goals and care preferences should guide which treatments to start, continue or stop; the evidence is promising but non-randomised.
claims_needing_evidence: Patient Priorities Care uses a facilitated conversation to identify health outcome goals and care preferences, which are shared with clinicians (JAMA Intern Med 2019; programme materials).

In a non-randomised trial in Connecticut primary care, Patient Priorities Care was associated with a reduction in perceived treatment burden and fewer medications or self-management tasks compared with usual care (JAMA Intern Med 2019).
evidence_leads: Tinetti ME et al. 2019, JAMA Intern Med 179:1688-97
patientprioritiescare.org
Tinetti ME, Naik AD, Dodson JA 2016, JAMA Cardiol, moving from disease-centered to patient goals-directed care (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Patient Priorities Care asks older people with several conditions two things: what they most want to be able to do, and what care they are willing and able to take on.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: two boxes (the person's goals; the person's care preferences) feeding into one treatment plan, with examples labelled 'Illustrative example' (goal: walk to the shops twice a week; preference: no more than one appointment a month).
candidates.pause: Clinicians juggling several disease guidelines for one person see a practical alternative.
candidates.gain: Two questions and a model with its evidence.
candidates.follow: Good care models explained with their evidence and limits.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E129 (ask what the person still wants in a frailty conversation). This post describes a specific tested method for aligning treatment with goals in multimorbidity.

candidates.working_title: If you have an ICD, ask about switching off the shocks
candidates.core_insight: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator can give shocks near the end of life that no longer help, and its shock function can be switched off painlessly without an operation, so people with an ICD can discuss in advance when that would be right.
candidates.angle: People with an ICD and their families often do not know the shock function can be turned off, or that doing so leaves ordinary pacing working; the conversation is easier before a crisis.
candidates.position: People with an ICD should be offered a conversation, well before the end of life, about when switching off the shocks would be right, and should know they can raise it themselves.
claims_needing_evidence: Some people with ICDs receive shocks in the last weeks and days of life (observational studies).
Discussions about deactivation often happen late or not at all (observational or family interview studies).
Deactivating the shock function is done without surgery using a programmer, is painless, and does not itself cause death; pacing can continue (BHF guidance; HRS and EHRA consensus statements).
A DNACPR decision does not automatically switch off an ICD (BHF guidance).
evidence_leads: British Heart Foundation, ICD deactivation at the end of life: principles and practice (with Resuscitation Council UK and National Council for Palliative Care; 2013, check for update)
Lampert R et al. 2010, Heart Rhythm 7:1008-26, HRS expert consensus
Padeletti L et al. 2010, Europace 12:1480-89, EHRA expert consensus
Goldstein NE et al. 2004, Ann Intern Med 141:835-38
Kinch Westerdahl A et al. 2014, Circulation 129:422-29
candidates.opening_line_draft: An implanted defibrillator can keep giving shocks when someone is dying. Its shock function can be switched off without an operation.
candidates.visual_idea: Drawn diagram of an ICD with two labelled functions (pacing; shocks) and an off-switch symbol on the shocks only, with a short list: painless, no operation, can be discussed in advance.
candidates.pause: Many families have never been told this, and the fact is striking without being graphic.
candidates.gain: Knowledge and a question to ask the cardiology or heart failure team.
candidates.follow: It explains decisions people can make in advance to avoid burdensome treatment.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Possible overlap with C19 (care near the end of life), to be resolved at allocation.

candidates.working_title: What the 3D trial found and did not find
candidates.core_insight: A large UK trial of patient-centred reviews for people with several long-term conditions did not improve quality of life scores, but did improve patients' reports of how person-centred and coordinated their care was.
candidates.angle: A null primary outcome is often read as 'it did not work'; here the intervention changed what patients experienced without shifting a generic quality of life score, which raises questions about the intervention, its delivery and the measure.
candidates.position: Patients' experience of coordinated care should be counted as an outcome in multimorbidity trials alongside quality of life, and a null primary result should be reported together with what did change.
claims_needing_evidence: The 3D trial randomised 33 general practices with [N to verify] patients who had three or more types of long-term condition (Lancet 2018).
There was no significant difference in the primary outcome, quality of life measured by EQ-5D-5L, at 15 months (Lancet 2018).
Patients in the intervention group reported more patient-centred care on secondary measures (Lancet 2018).
Not all intervention patients received the full planned reviews (Lancet 2018 or process evaluation).
evidence_leads: Salisbury C et al. 2018, Lancet 392:41-50, 3D approach cluster randomised trial
Mann C et al. 2019, process evaluation of the 3D trial (unsure)
NICE NG56 Multimorbidity
candidates.opening_line_draft: A UK trial of patient-centred reviews for people with several long-term conditions did not improve quality of life scores. Patients still reported better care.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison chart from verified data: the primary outcome (no clear difference, with its uncertainty stated in words) beside patient-reported experience measures (improved), with labels and denominators, and a plain box on what a null primary outcome does and does not mean.
candidates.pause: Practitioners interested in multimorbidity care may know the trial only as 'negative'.
candidates.gain: A more careful reading of a well-known null trial.
candidates.follow: It reads evidence fairly, including null results.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Possible overlap with C20 (measurement), to be resolved at allocation.
